【ETHICS STATEMENT · imt270187-sec-0130-p1】Participation was voluntary, and questionnaire completion after disclosure of the study purpose constituted implied consent. Optional email addresses, names, and affiliations were excluded from the primary analyses and used only for limited post hoc matching to public professional records. The primary analyses used de‐identified data, and only aggregate findings are reported. Under local institutional policy, formal ethics approval was not required for this minimal‐risk survey.

【IMPLEMENTATION STAGES AND TRANSLATION GAP · imt270187-sec-0040-p1】Recorded implementation indicators varied across technology domains and self‐rated experience groups (Figure 1D). For spatial transcriptomics, regular use was reported by 41 of 239 respondents (17.2%). Group‐specific proportions were higher among dual‐domain experts (42.9%) and spatial biology experts (32.6%) than among non‐experts (1.6%). For 3D imaging, regular or occasional use was reported by 55 of 239 respondents (23.0%), comprising 66.7% of 3D pathology experts, 58.9% of dual‐domain experts, 9.4% of non‐experts, and 8.7% of spatial biology experts (Tables S5 and S7). These percentages use the full cohort or group as the denominator and describe recorded use. No feedback was recorded for 83 respondents (34.7%) in Question 5.2, as shown in Figure S5B and reported separately in Table S7, and was not interpreted as confirmed non‐implementation. A mean item‐level engagement indicator derived from Questions 6.1 and 6.2 was highest among dual‐domain experts (87.5%), followed by spatial biology experts (81.5%), 3D pathology experts (72.2%), and non‐experts (36.3%). This two‐item average uses full‐group denominators and is not a percentage of unique engaged respondents. These unadjusted summaries describe variation in reported use and engagement across the operational categories of self‐rated domain experience.

【SURVEY COHORT AND EXPERTISE COMPOSITION · imt270187-sec-0020-p1】The survey included 239 respondents. Most were based in Asia (73.2%, n = 175), primarily mainland China (25.1%, n = 60), Singapore (14.6%, n = 35), and India (9.6%, n = 23) (Figure 1B; Figure S1A). Respondents were classified as spatial biology experts (19.2%), 3D pathology experts (3.8%), dual‐domain experts (23.4%), or non‐experts (53.6%) (Figure S1B). ASDP members accounted for 21.3% (n = 51) (Figure S1C). Pathologists represented the largest professional group (44.8%, n = 107) (Figure S1D).

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Asia-enriched survey of spatial biology and three-dimensional pathology》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【EXPLORATORY STATISTICAL ANALYSES · imt270187-sec-0070-p1】Early‐late respondents (120/119) differed in professional role and self‐rated experience after Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) and Benjamini–Yekutieli (BY) correction (Table S1). The non‐expert late‐minus‐early difference was 32.2 percentage points (pointwise 95% confidence interval (CI), 19.7–43.3). Experience composition also differed across four chronological blocks after correction. Among 84 exploratory comparisons (Tables S2–S6), 55 met BH and 42 BY thresholds; all are reported. Table S7 summarizes marker multiplexing and 3D imaging use. Comparisons without covariate adjustment cannot establish an independent contribution of experience to implementation. These chronological comparisons cannot quantify or exclude non‐response bias.

【DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENT · imt270187-sec-0120-p1】The summary statistics supporting the findings of this study are provided in the article and its Supporting Information. De‐identified respondent‐level survey data are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhuzhu1986/Wang-Zhengyang. The full survey questionnaire is included in the Supporting Information. Names, email addresses, affiliations, and other identifying information are excluded from the shared data to protect participant confidentiality. Supplementary materials (figures, tables, methods, graphical abstract, slides, videos, Chinese translated version, and updated materials) may be found in the online DOI or iMeta Science http://www.imeta.science/.

【FIGURE 1 · imt270187-fig-0001】FIGURE 1 Survey cohort, geographic distribution, and expertise‐stratified adoption landscape. (A) Survey design and cohort overview of the Asia‐enriched global web‐based survey. The survey involved participation by members of the Asian Society of Digital Pathology (ASDP) and the European Society of Digital and Integrative Pathology (ESDIP). Society logos are used with permission to denote member participation. (B) Geographic distribution of the leading contributing countries/regions, with respondent counts and percentages. (C) Relative engagement in spatial transcriptomics, multiplex spatial imaging, three‐dimensional (3D) pathology, and multimodal integration, stratified by expertise group. (D) Implementation indicators for regular use of spatial transcriptomics, implemented use of 3D imaging, and the mean item‐level engagement indicator for Questions 6.1 and 6.2. The latter is calculated as 100 × (Question 6.1‐positive respondents + Question 6.2‐positive respondents)/(2 × group size), with respondents counted once per item. No feedback contributes no recorded positive and remains in the denominator; the indicator is not a percentage of unique engaged respondents.

【FIGURE 2 · imt270187-fig-0002】FIGURE 2 Barriers, bottlenecks, and translational priorities. (A) Cross‐domain barriers to the implementation of spatial transcriptomics, multiplex imaging, and three‐dimensional (3D) pathology. (B) Leading domain‐specific bottlenecks for spatial transcriptomics, multiplex imaging, and 3D pathology. (C) Future technological priorities and expected high‐impact biomedical applications. (D) Confidence in the clinical translation of spatial biology and 3D pathology within the next decade, stratified by expertise group. In panel D, no feedback is shown separately, and percentages use full‐cohort or full‐group denominators. Ordered confidence comparisons exclude no feedback and include 207 valid responses: 46 spatial biology experts, 9 3D pathology experts, 55 dual‐domain experts, and 97 non‐experts. AI, artificial intelligence; TME, tumor microenvironment.
